description: A young boy who loves space. This boy loves space and built SimSphere, a working mission simulator where AI agents check launch, cost, debris and weather to give a GO / NO-GO verdict. We’re taking on the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning it into a game where players design missions, earn scores and learn why real missions succeed or fail. Looking for a Spanish speaker to help
summary:
I designed Mission: Beyond Earth, a browser game where you run a complete space mission from start to finish. You design a wildfire-watching satellite on a $13.8M budget, choosing its camera, solar panels, battery and antenna, where every part costs money, mass and power. Then you launch it from a 3D cockpit with real physics: Max Q, staging, fairing jettison and a two-burn insertion into a polar orbit. Finally, you operate it for one day over Europe using real NASA FIRMS fire detections, managing Earth’s shadow, battery power, onboard storage and ground-station downlinks.

The debrief links every design choice to the result. A cheaper camera misses fires at night, too few solar panels drain the battery, and a slow antenna leaves firefighters waiting. That’s exactly what the challenge asks for: engineering decisions, limited resources, and seeing how each choice shapes success.

It matters because you learn by doing, not by reading a lesson first.

I came up with the idea, the mission flow, the gameplay and every design decision. I used Claude (an AI assistant) to help write and test the code under my direction.
details:
Mission: Beyond Earth is a browser game where you run a full space mission. First you design a wildfire-watching satellite on a $13.8M budget, choosing its camera, solar panels, battery and antenna. Every part costs money, mass and power. Then you launch it from a 3D cockpit with real rocket physics. Finally, you operate it for one day over Europe using real NASA FIRMS fire data, dealing with Earth’s shadow, battery power and sending pictures to ground stations.

At the end, the debrief shows how each choice changed the result, like a cheap camera missing fires at night or a slow antenna making firefighters wait. Players learn real engineering trade-offs by playing, not by reading.

I built it with HTML, JavaScript and three.js, and it runs in any browser with no install. I made it realistic but easy to start, with a Cadet mode (autopilot) and a Commander mode (full control).
